# Appendix A: Methods and Techniques {.unnumbered}

Brief explanations of techniques that appear in the two anchor articles and in the course activities. Each entry follows the same pattern so you can add to it: **What it is**, **What it measures**, **Typical controls**, **Watch out for**, and **Resources**. Add your own explanations and links to any **Resources** line.

::: {.callout-tip}
## How to read a method
For every technique ask: What is the **variable**? What is the **control**? What is the **readout**? Then record it on a Method Card (see Sand Fly Module 3).
:::

## A.1 Microbiology techniques

### Isolating and culturing a bacterium {#m-culture}

- **What it is:** growing a microbe from a sample (for example, a mosquito or sand fly gut) on a medium until single colonies can be picked and purified.
- **What it measures:** whether a bacterium is present and can be grown; colonies can be counted as colony-forming units (CFU).
- **Typical controls:** uninoculated media; samples from untreated insects.
- **Watch out for:** microbes that grow poorly in the lab, and contamination from the environment.
- **Used in:** Section 1 (isolating TC1 from mosquitoes) and Section 2 (colonization of sand fly midguts).
- **Resources:** @sharma2026 for *Delftia* background; the Methods of each anchor article for how isolates and CFU counts were handled.

### Gram staining and microscopy {#m-gram}

- **What it is:** a stain that separates bacteria by cell-wall type. Gram-negative cells do not keep the purple dye. Cell shape is then viewed under a microscope.
- **What it measures:** Gram reaction and cell shape (for *Delftia*: Gram-negative rods).
- **Watch out for:** over-decolorizing, which can make Gram-positive cells look Gram-negative.
- **Resources:** @smith2005 (ASM Microbe Library).

### 16S rRNA gene sequencing {#m-16s}

- **What it is:** reading the sequence of a conserved bacterial gene to place an isolate on the tree of life.
- **What it measures:** relatedness; it was the basis for placing *Delftia* in its own genus (@wen1999) and for describing *D. tsuruhatensis* (@shigematsu2003).
- **Watch out for:** 16S alone may not separate closely related species; it usually identifies the genus well but is less reliable for species (@janda2007).
- **Resources:** NCBI BLAST [@ncbi_blast] (choose Nucleotide BLAST, then the "16S ribosomal RNA sequences (Bacteria and Archaea)" database); @janda2007.

## A.2 Vector and parasite experiments

### Feeding insects bacteria, supernatant or a compound {#m-feeding}

- **What it is:** giving mosquitoes or sand flies a bacterial suspension, the bacterium-free culture supernatant, or a purified compound in sugar or a blood meal, at a chosen time before or after infection.
- **What it measures:** whether the bacterium, or something it secretes, changes infection.
- **Typical controls:** insects fed sugar or medium only; supernatant versus live bacteria to separate secreted factors from live colonization.
- **Example (Section 2):** @cecilio2025 fed *P. duboscqi* sand flies about 10^8 CFU/ml bacteria in 5% sucrose on cotton rolls for 24 h, at 1 week or 24 h before infection, or 5 or 8 days after. Comparisons included live versus dead TC1, GFP-labeled TC1, bacterium-free supernatant, *E. coli* and a bacterium isolated from sand fly midguts.
- **Watch out for:** timing (before or after infection) can change the result, so Cecilio et al. varied it.
- **Resources:** the Methods sections of @huang2023 and @cecilio2025 (see References).

### Infection assays and parasite counts {#m-infection}

- **What it is:** infecting insects with a parasite (*Plasmodium falciparum* in Section 1; *Leishmania major* in Section 2), then dissecting tissues to count parasite stages. In mosquitoes these include oocysts on the midgut and sporozoites in the salivary glands.
- **What it measures:** infection prevalence (how many insects are infected) and intensity (how many parasites per insect).
- **Typical controls:** untreated, infected insects; a different bacterium or a non-colonized group.
- **Example (Section 2):** sand flies were infected with *L. major* by artificial membrane feeding. In one experiment infection prevalence was 30.9% in bacteria-fed flies versus 51.2% in controls (relative risk 0.65) [@cecilio2025].
- **Watch out for:** prevalence and intensity can change independently; report both.
- **Resources:** CDC malaria life cycle [@cdc_malaria_lifecycle] (includes the mosquito stages: ookinete, oocyst, sporozoite); WHO leishmaniasis fact sheet [@who_leishmaniasis]; WHO malaria fact sheet [@who_malaria].

### Gut colonization and fitness assays {#m-colonization}

- **What it is:** measuring whether a bacterium persists in the insect gut over time and whether it harms the host (for example, survival, egg laying, development).
- **What it measures:** stability of colonization and cost to the host.
- **Why it matters:** a candidate control agent must persist and should not harm the vector. Huang et al. [-@huang2023] report that TC1 stably populates the mosquito gut without a fitness cost. @cecilio2025 report that TC1 colonizes the sand fly midgut, likely disrupts the gut microbiota (dysbiosis), and that colonized, *Leishmania*-infected flies show increased mortality.
- **Watch out for:** a fitness cost to the vector changes both the biology and the modeling.
- **Resources:** the Results and Discussion of the two anchor articles (see References).

### Dose-response and IC50 {#m-ic50}

- **What it is:** testing a compound at several concentrations and finding the concentration that gives a half-maximal effect (IC50).
- **What it measures:** potency. @huang2023 report an IC50 of 46 nM for harmane against oocyst formation.
- **Watch out for:** a lower IC50 means a more potent compound; units matter (nM versus µM).
- **Resources:** the harmane dose-response data in @huang2023; PubChem entry for harmane (listed as "harman") [@pubchem_harmane].

## A.3 Chemistry and imaging

### Identifying a secreted molecule (bioassay-guided fractionation) {#m-fractionation}

- **What it is:** separating a culture supernatant into fractions, testing each for activity, and repeating until a single active compound can be identified with analytical chemistry (typically mass spectrometry and nuclear magnetic resonance).
- **What it measures:** which molecule is responsible for an effect.
- **Used in:** Section 1 (identifying harmane as the TC1 inhibitor).
- **Resources:** PubChem [@pubchem_harmane] (structure and properties of harmane, a methylated β-carboline); @huang2023.

### Electron and light microscopy {#m-microscopy}

- **What it is:** imaging bacteria or tissue at high magnification to see size, shape and location.
- **What it measures:** morphology and where a microbe sits in the insect. @huang2023 report TC1 cells from 0.7 to 4.2 µm wide, some up to 24 µm long, suggesting a large space occupancy in mosquito cavities.
- **Resources:** Fig. 1 of @huang2023; @cecilio2025 for GFP-labeled TC1 in sand fly guts.

## A.4 Field studies and modeling

### Contained field studies {#m-field}

- **What it is:** testing an intervention under realistic conditions, such as a sugar bait or treated breeding site, in a setting that prevents release into the environment.
- **What it measures:** whether lab results hold up outside the lab.
- **Used in:** Section 1 (Burkina Faso).
- **Details:** TC1 was introduced orally from sugar baits or by seeding breeding sites, and mosquitoes carrying it suppressed development of locally circulating *P. falciparum* [@huang2023].
- **Watch out for:** small scale and local conditions limit generalization.
- **Resources:** @huang2023, field studies section.

### Mathematical modeling and R0 {#m-modeling}

- **What it is:** a simulation of how infection spreads, using inputs such as biting rate and the proportion of insects carrying the bacterium. The basic reproduction number (R0) is the average number of new infections caused by one infection in a susceptible population; below 1 an outbreak fades.
- **What it measures:** the predicted public-health effect of an intervention. @huang2023 report that introducing TC1 could avert about 15% of additional clinical malaria cases. @cecilio2025 model R0, accounting for the higher mortality of colonized, infected sand flies, and predict R0 falling below 1 in some modeled settings.
- **Watch out for:** outputs depend on assumptions. Audit them (see Sand Fly Module 5).
- **Resources:** the modeling sections and supplements of both anchor articles (see References).

## A.5 Statistics and data analysis

### Reading error bars, replicates and effect size {#m-statistics}

- **What it is:** judging how reliable and how large a difference is, not only whether it is "significant".
- **What to check:** number of independent replicates; what error bars show (standard deviation, standard error or confidence interval); effect size; and whether the statistical test fits the data.
- **Resources:** @cumming2007

## A.6 Course techniques {#m-course}

| Technique | Purpose | Where used |
|---|---|---|
| Concept map | Surface prior knowledge and gaps | Sand Fly Module 1 |
| Source-reliability check (who, reviewed, recent, evidence) | Judge sources for the portfolio | Sand Fly Modules 1–2 |
| Data Analysis Sheet (DAS) | Record question, controls, readout, result, assumptions, implications for each figure | Module 4–5; Sand Fly Modules 4–5 |
| Claim–evidence–reasoning (CER) | Write evidence-based arguments | Module 6; Sand Fly Module 6 |
| Next-experiment aims page | Propose a testable follow-up | Module 7; Sand Fly Module 7 |

C.R.E.A.T.E. method sources: @hoskins2007 and [@teachcreate].
